lines.text: In November twenty twenty-six, Amazon warned New York shoppers that a proposed city law, the Delivery Protection Act, could add up to five dollars to every order.
The bill would make large delivery companies get a city license and hire their drivers directly, instead of contracting with local delivery firms, along with new rules on firing, training and safety.

The mayor, Zohran Mamdani, answered on X. "Amazon is a multi-trillion dollar company. If Jeff Bezos adds five dollars to your order, it's not because of City Council's efforts to protect workers' rights and keep our streets safe. It's greed."

Start with who actually pays. If Amazon isn't allowed to pass the cost on, as the mayor demands, it lands on whoever owns the shares: Jeff Bezos, sure, but also a retired couple living off a pension fund, and someone fresh out of college with a first index fund. A company's size says nothing about how rich any one of its owners is. It's a tax, just an invisible one. Hold that thought. We'll see the exact same move again, with a landlord.

And look at what kind of help this is. Holding down Amazon's prices is a benefit you can only spend at Amazon, handed to whoever happens to shop there, rich or poor. Help that's only good for one thing, paid for by a tax nobody can see. That's the mistake this whole video is about.
Here's the claim this video is going to defend. Nearly every policy on the socialist menu is the same mistake, repeated over and over. Once you see the mistake, you can't unsee it.
But first, a warning, because you're going to think you know where this is going. You probably don't.
When someone attacks socialism, you know the script. Taxes are theft. Handouts make people lazy. Cut the safety net.
That's not the argument we're making.
This video takes no position on how much we should help the poor. More than now, less than now, none at all. That's a question of values, and you're entitled to your own answer.
Our question is narrower, and a lot harder to wriggle out of. Whatever amount of help you've decided on, what's the least wasteful way to deliver it?

Picture the economy as a pie. Growing the pie is one goal. Sharing it is another. Most political fights assume you have to trade one for the other. This video is about sharing the pie, however much you want to share, without shrinking it any more than you have to.
If at any point you think you hear the case for cutting welfare, you don't. That's not the argument we're making, and we'll keep saying so.

And this is why criticism of these policies usually falls flat. It tends to come from conservatives and libertarians, and it goes like this. Rent control is a disaster. Scrap it. Scrap the minimum wage. Scrap the food stamps.
And replace them with nothing.
To a voter who wants to help people, "replace it with nothing" sounds exactly like "I don't want to help people." And the socialist on social media gets to say: you think kids shouldn't eat?

Take the minimum wage. The evidence on moderate increases is mixed. Some studies find meaningful job losses. Others find almost none. It's at least plausible that, up to a point, what a modest minimum wage does for low earners outweighs the harm it does to the wider economy.
We're not going to pretend otherwise. If your only choices were a modest minimum wage or nothing, the minimum wage might win.
But those aren't your only choices. That's the whole point.
You'll hear a phrase thrown at anyone who criticizes these policies. Trickle-down economics.

Let's be precise about what it means, because almost nobody is. The trickle-down claim is this: if you scrap some policy that gets in the market's way, the economy grows enough that even the people who were being helped come out ahead. The efficiency gain outweighs the lost equity.
Sometimes that's true. For rent control, it may well be true. Scrap it, more housing gets built, rents fall, and many tenants end up better off.

But it isn't true everywhere, automatically. And that's where the usual left-right fight gets stuck. One side says grow the pie, even if it's shared less evenly. The other says share the pie, even if it shrinks. They argue about where to set one knob: more sharing and a smaller pie, or a bigger pie and less sharing.
We're turning a different knob entirely.
Hold the amount of redistribution fixed. Exactly the same amount of help, going to exactly the same people. Now ask: can we deliver it with less waste?
Almost always, yes. And nobody loses their help.

Picture redistribution as a pipe, carrying money from people who have more to people who have less. Every restriction and every hidden cost is a hole in that pipe, and money leaks out on the way. The trickle-down crowd looks at the leaks and says: shrink the pipe, or shut it off. We're saying: fix the leaks, whatever size you want the pipe to be.

We'll say it once more, for the people already drafting an angry comment. Same redistribution. Less waste. If you hear that as an argument for cutting welfare, you've just made the exact mistake this video is about.

In twenty eighteen, the Niskanen Center published a paper by Samuel Hammond with a title that sounds like an oxymoron: The Free-Market Welfare State. Look at the two knobs, and it isn't one. Turn the how-much knob as high as you like. Keep the how knob on open markets and cash.
So if replacing these programs with nothing isn't the answer, what is? There's a third option, and one of the clearest ways to see it comes from the right.

Take food stamps. For most families, they already work almost like cash, because most families spend more on groceries than the benefit is worth anyway. Where they don't, it's because of the rules, like the ban on hot meals.

Starting in twenty twenty-five, the Trump administration approved state after state's request to add more rules: no soda, no candy. Florida even banned packaged desserts, the cookies and snack cakes almost everyone enjoys now and then. Progressives called it paternalism, and they were right. And notice how easily they saw it. Nobody compared the dessert ban to having no food stamps at all. They compared it to the same food stamps, without the ban. The right baseline was obvious.
lines.say: [dryly] Starting in twenty twenty-five, the Trump administration approved state after state's request to add more rules: no soda, no candy. Florida even banned packaged desserts, the cookies and snack cakes almost everyone enjoys now and then. Progressives called it paternalism, and they were right. And notice how easily they saw it. Nobody compared the dessert ban to having no food stamps at all. They compared it to the same food stamps, without the ban. The right baseline was obvious.

lines.text: Here's the key identity. Any benefit in kind is just cash, with a restriction on how you can spend it. A hundred dollars in food stamps is a hundred dollars, plus one restriction: groceries only. The dessert ban just adds another. And a restriction on how you spend your own benefit can never give you more choices. By definition, it can only take them away.

So when you object to the dessert ban, you're not objecting to the help. You're objecting to the restriction. Drop it, and the family keeps every dollar, with more choices. That's all we're saying. Now use that baseline everywhere. Compare rent control, city grocery stores and free-but-only-for-this programs, not to nothing, but to the same help with no strings attached. Republicans didn't trust poor families to pick their own groceries, and progressives rightly objected. So why trust them any less to pick their own apartment?
This pattern is so common it deserves a name: helping people with one specific thing instead of money. Call it the gift card fallacy.

And it usually isn't a belief anyone states out loud. It's a reflex. People need housing, so give them housing. People need food, so give them food. The alternative, the same help with no strings attached, never even comes to mind. So the gift card gets measured against the wrong baseline: not against cash, but against nothing. Call it the false baseline.
Here's what the false baseline hides. Picture an actual gift. The loss it causes has a name: deadweight loss.

Say I buy you a sweater for ten dollars. How much is it worth to you? We don't have to guess. Offer you a choice: keep the sweater, or take cash instead. The smallest amount of cash you'd accept in its place is what it's worth to you. Say it's seven dollars. Economists call that revealed preference: your own choice tells us the value.
So I've spent ten dollars, and you've gained something worth seven. The other three dollars just disappeared. I didn't get them. You didn't get them. Nobody did.
lines.say: [calmly] So I've spent ten dollars, and you've gained something worth seven. The other three dollars just disappeared. I didn't get them. You didn't get them. Nobody did.

lines.text: This isn't a thought experiment. The economist Joel Waldfogel asked people what cash they'd have accepted in place of each holiday gift they received, and found that somewhere between a tenth and a third of what givers spent simply evaporated.

To be fair, a holiday gift carries things cash can't: the thought behind it, the ritual, the people around the tree. Nobody's saying you should mail your grandmother a check. But none of that sentiment comes with a housing voucher. You're not sipping eggnog with Uncle Sam.
lines.say: [warmly] To be fair, a holiday gift carries things cash can't: the thought behind it, the ritual, the people around the tree. Nobody's saying you should mail your grandmother a check. But none of that sentiment comes with a housing voucher. You're not sipping eggnog with Uncle Sam.

lines.text: If I'd handed you a ten-dollar bill instead, nothing would have been lost. That missing three dollars is deadweight loss. Value that could have existed, but doesn't.
Every gift card is the sweater. The family receives something worth less to them than what it cost to provide. The gap vanishes.

This part isn't a matter of opinion. Give the family the cash instead. If they'd have bought exactly what the gift card buys, the gift card was only as good as cash. If they'd buy something else, then by their own choice, that something else was worth more to them. Either way, cash is at least as good. It is never worse.

Now make it concrete. Say you land a rent-stabilized apartment. You'd rather live somewhere cheaper, so you sublet it at the market rate, move, and spend the difference on whatever your family needs most. You're better off. Your subtenant, who chose to pay that rent, is better off too.

That's against the rules. In New York, subletting a rent-stabilized apartment for more than the legal rent, plus a small surcharge if it's furnished, can get you evicted and leave you owing your subtenant up to three times the overcharge. Try it with a public housing unit, and you can lose the unit.

Why should that be illegal? Notice what the sublet does: it turns the discount into its cash value. Economically, it's identical to the city simply handing you the money. So refusing to give people cash comes with an enforcement arm. When someone converts their gift card into cash on their own, you punish them for it.

That's a move we'll use again and again: take two arrangements that look completely different, and show that the money moves exactly the same way in both. Call it economic physics. Once you see the identity, what was hidden becomes visible.

The usual objection to cash is that the poor will waste it. That's been tested, a lot. A World Bank review of nineteen studies found that when poor families get cash, spending on alcohol and tobacco doesn't go up. If anything, it goes down.

To be fair, there are real exceptions. Some things nobody can be fenced out of, like national defense, or a lighthouse guiding every ship that passes. You can't sell those one customer at a time, so government has to provide them directly. And sometimes the person holding the cash isn't the person we're trying to help, like a child. Those cases are real. They're also narrow.
Now watch how far the pattern goes.

A public housing lottery. Win it, and you get one particular apartment, in one particular building, in one particular neighborhood. Almost certainly not the one you'd have picked if you'd been handed the money. Gift card.

The same goes for rules that make it hard to end a lease, or costly to let a worker go. They feel like the decent, humane thing, and you'd seem heartless to question them. But compare them to the right baseline. Each one is a benefit you can only spend on one thing: staying in that apartment, or keeping that job. Nobody protected by them can choose to take it as cash instead.

Free street parking. Curb space in a city is some of the most valuable land on earth, handed out free to whoever owns a car. In Japan, by contrast, you generally can't register a car without proof of an off-street space to keep it in, and parking on the street overnight is mostly banned. There, parking is something you pay for, like anything else. Here, it's a gift card for drivers.

Even public libraries. Most people like them, and they do some things cash can't, like letting many readers share one copy of a book. But make the trade-off explicit. In the twenty twenty-three to twenty twenty-four fiscal year, San Francisco's library system spent about two hundred million dollars. That's roughly two hundred and fifty dollars for every resident, about a thousand dollars a year for a family of four, or about fifty dollars for every visit through the doors. Offer every family that cash instead, and ask how many would still pick the library. That's the question a gift card never asks.

City-owned grocery stores, which wouldn't pay rent or property tax. Those waived costs are a subsidy, delivered only to people who live near one of the stores and want to shop there. Why not give people the money and let them shop wherever they like? Gift card, with a location attached.

Fare-free buses. This one gets partial credit. Buses take cars off the road, and fewer cars means less traffic and pollution for everyone. That's a real case for subsidizing them. But zero fares go to every rider, rich or poor, and the cleaner fix is charging drivers for the congestion and pollution they cause. A gift card with a half-decent excuse.

Which brings us back to Amazon. Some of the delivery law, like training and safety standards, might address real problems. You can't easily check how well a driver was trained, and reckless driving puts everyone on the street at risk. Fair enough. But the core of the bill is forcing companies to hire drivers as employees instead of contractors. That doesn't hand drivers money. It hands them a fixed package of job terms, help they can only take in one form, whether or not it's the form they'd have chosen.
Policy after policy, take it apart and you find the same machine inside: help delivered in kind instead of cash. Help with strings attached.
So before we go further, here's the alternative in a nutshell.
Whatever amount of help you want to give, give it as cash. The same check to every citizen.
Same help, far less waste. How to pay for it without creating new waste is the other half of the story.

So far, we've looked at the benefit side: help that's only good for one thing. Now look at the other side of the ledger. Every subsidy and every price control comes with a bill, and somebody pays it. The trick is that the bill is usually hidden. So let's make it visible.

Take that free street parking. People assume it costs nothing, because the city already owns the curb. But if the city charged what that land is worth, it could collect that money and cut some other tax by the same amount. Giving the curb away means everyone pays higher taxes to cover it. A dollar not collected is a dollar that has to be raised somewhere else.
Before the biggest bill of all, a quick word on terms, because someone in the comments is already typing.

What is socialism, exactly? Even its founders weren't tidy about it. Marx and Engels used socialism and communism loosely, and over their careers applied both words to their own ideas. The neat version, where socialism is a waystation on the road to communism, came later, mostly from Lenin.

People use the word for everything from Soviet five-year plans to Scandinavian welfare states. So forget the dictionary. Look at what self-described socialists actually campaign on: rent freezes, city-run grocery stores, fare-free buses, and mandates like that delivery law.
Add the rest of the usual menu. Price controls, like rent control and the minimum wage. Nationalized industries. Benefits handed out in kind instead of in cash.

Underneath every item is the same move: replace a price the market would set with a decision made politically. Rent control is a city official deciding what an apartment is allowed to cost. That's central planning, one building at a time.
Rent control. The flagship policy, on the platform of self-described socialists almost everywhere.
So take one. Market rent, three thousand dollars a month. Controlled rent, two thousand.
The tenant saves a thousand dollars a month. Where does that thousand come from?
Not from the city. Not from taxpayers. It comes out of one person's pocket: whoever happened to own that particular building.

So rent control is a thousand-dollar housing voucher, funded by a thousand-dollar tax on one landlord, chosen more or less at random. Propose that policy in those words, and almost nobody would vote for it. Rent control is the same policy, under a friendlier name.
To see why that kind of tax does so much damage, look at what any tax on a trade does. When two people trade freely, both expect to come out ahead, or they'd walk away.

Economists have a name for a change that makes someone better off and nobody worse off. A Pareto improvement. It's the one kind of change you can call good without weighing one person's happiness against another's.

Every voluntary trade is a little Pareto improvement. Say Dana would fix your roof for twenty dollars an hour, and you'd happily pay twenty-five. The job happens, and five dollars of value appears out of nowhere, split between you.
Now put an eight-dollar tax on that hour of work. Dana needs twenty-eight to make it worthwhile. You'll only pay twenty-five. The job never happens.
The government collects nothing. Dana loses the work. Your roof still leaks. And five dollars of value never comes into existence.

And notice this isn't a judgment call. Nobody forced either of you into that deal. The fact that you both chose it is proof that you both came out ahead. That's revealed preference again. Which means a tax that blocks a useful trade like that one makes the world worse, by definition.
So there are two leaks. Benefits worth less than they cost, which we saw with every gift card. And taxes that kill trades that would have happened. The socialist toolkit is built out of both.

And notice what rent control can't live without. If the landlord could simply decline to renew the lease, the discount would vanish at the end of the year. So rent control always comes with eviction control. In New York, a rent-stabilized tenant has a legal right to renew, and the landlord can't end the lease just because the rent is below market. The thousand-dollar tax never expires.
And it gets worse, because people respond.

The tenant's discount only works in this one apartment. So they stay put long after it suits them. The job across town, the bigger place for the new baby, the smaller place after the kids leave. All of it now costs a thousand dollars a month in lost discount.

Landlords respond too. When economists studied rent control in San Francisco, they found landlords cut the supply of rental housing by fifteen percent, by converting buildings to condos and redeveloping them. Which pushed up rents for everyone who didn't already have a controlled unit.
When leading economists were surveyed on whether rent control had made housing more affordable in the cities that tried it, almost none agreed. This is about as close to consensus as economics gets.
So rent control fails both tests. It's a benefit worth less than it costs, and it's a tax that kills trades. A double leak.

The same goes for that delivery law. Making every driver a direct employee piles fixed costs onto every hire. For many drivers, the job still works. But at the margin, some hires stop penciling out, and deliveries that both sides wanted never happen. That's the roof, all over again.

Now, back to that word the mayor used. Greed. Notice the move. New rules about how deliveries must be run cost money to follow. But according to the mayor, the law can't be the reason prices go up. And if they go up anyway, that's greed.

Sit with that for a second. To the mayor, absorbing the cost is just the decent thing to do, the default. Time for a little economic physics. Charge a customer five dollars less than you could, or charge full price and mail them a five-dollar check. Run the books both ways, and the company ends the year with exactly the same money, and so does the customer. Absorbing a cost you could pass on is a donation.

So the accusation isn't that Amazon takes something from anyone. Nobody ends up worse off than they were. The accusation is that its owners failed to give enough away. We don't usually call people greedy for skipping a donation. And if we're going to demand charity, why aim it at whoever happens to be shopping online, rather than people who need it far more?

We don't usually call people greedy for skipping a donation. And if we're going to demand charity, why aim it at whoever happens to be shopping online, rather than people who need it far more?

lines.text: Here's another way to see it. Say I own an antique lamp worth maybe five hundred dollars, and I list it for a million. That's absurd. But am I hurting anyone? Am I taking anything from someone who needs a lamp? No. I'm offering a trade, and nobody has to take it. Asking too much is just a bad offer. It isn't theft.

In fact, you do this every day. If someone offered you three million dollars for your house, you'd probably move out. At some price, almost anyone would sell. So every day you keep it, you're holding out for more than any buyer is offering. If that's greed, then everyone who owns anything is greedy, and the only escape is to keep giving until you're as poor as the next poorest person. Follow the word far enough, and it stops meaning anything.
Every time there's a storm, a strike, or a wave of cancelled flights, the same outrage cycle kicks off. Uber triples its prices. Gouging! Greed! Somebody pass a law.
So think about the night the flights get grounded. Thousands of stranded travelers open the app at once. There are only so many cars.
Who should get one? The traveler stuck at the airport at midnight with a sick kid, or the guy running an errand he could just as easily do tomorrow?
You can't tell them apart by looking. Neither can Uber. But the price can. At triple the fare, the errand waits until tomorrow, and the car goes to someone whose trip can't wait.
And the price does something else. It tells the driver who was planning to stay home tonight that tonight is the night to work. A surge rations the cars, and it summons more of them.
Cap the price, and both effects vanish. The cars go to whoever taps first. The extra drivers stay home. The stranded family waits.

Here's the thing nobody says. Surge pricing is just happy hour, viewed from the other direction. A bar cuts its prices at four in the afternoon because the place is empty. Which means the regular price on a Friday night is the surge price. Nobody calls that greed. It's one signal, pointing both ways: come now, there's room, or only come now if it matters. And drivers, please show up.
lines.say: [dryly] Here's the thing nobody says. Surge pricing is just happy hour, viewed from the other direction. A bar cuts its prices at four in the afternoon because the place is empty. Which means the regular price on a Friday night is the surge price. Nobody calls that greed. It's one signal, pointing both ways: come now, there's room, or only come now if it matters. And drivers, please show up.

lines.text: And if what bothers you is that a poor family can't afford the surge, fine. That's a real concern about equity. Which is a case for giving that family more money, every day of the year. Breaking the one signal that gets cars to the people who need them helps nobody.
A price cap is a discount for whoever's quickest, paid for by everyone left stranded. Gift card fallacy. Again.

Economists call this rationing by price versus rationing by waiting. Free roads ration by waiting. That's why Houston widened the Katy Freeway to as many as twenty-six lanes, and within a few years, rush-hour trips took longer than before. Free lanes just fill up. When New York started charging drivers to enter the busiest part of Manhattan in twenty twenty-five, traffic dropped and trips got faster, and plenty of progressives cheered. That's surge pricing, for roads.
So how do you share the pie without shrinking it? Economics has a result for exactly this, and it's been sitting in the textbooks for decades. The second welfare theorem.

In its ideal form, it says you can reach any distribution of resources you like, a little sharing or a lot, without shrinking the economy at all, as long as the money moves in ways that don't depend on what anyone does.
Real life never gets that perfect. But we can get much closer than any gift card ever will.
And this splits one fight into two. How much to share is a question of values. How to share is a question of engineering. And engineering has better and worse answers.
Start with taxes that don't block useful trades. There are two big ones.
Pollution first. When a factory dumps smoke on its neighbors for free, it produces too much, because someone else is paying part of the bill. Economists call that a negative externality.

A pollution tax hands the bill back to the polluter. And here's the remarkable part: this tax removes deadweight loss. The economy was producing too much smoke, and the tax pulls it back toward the right amount. The economist Arthur Pigou worked this out over a century ago, which is why these are called Pigouvian taxes. A tax that makes the pie bigger.
Next, land. Picture an empty lot. A train station opens nearby. Then shops, then a hospital, then thousands of neighbors. The lot is suddenly worth far more.
The owner didn't do any of that. The value soaked into the lot from everything around it. It's a positive externality, created by everyone else, captured by whoever holds the deed.

Now tax that land value. Look at who pays: the owner. Now look at who created the value: the train station, the shops, the hospital, the neighbors. The person paying the tax isn't the one whose work leaked into the land. And the bill is the same whether they build, sell, work, or sit in a lawn chair. Nothing they do changes it. No trade gets blocked. No deadweight loss.

How far can these two go? Further than most people think. Henry George argued in eighteen seventy-nine that a land tax alone could fund the government. Here's why that's plausible. Scrap the taxes on wages and sales, and people have more money to spend. Much of it ends up competing for the same places to live and work, and that competition pushes up the rental value of land. So the land tax brings in more, and it still doesn't block a single trade.

To the extent that still falls short, add one flat tax on consumption, with as few loopholes as possible. That part does block some trades. It shrinks the pie a little. So keep it as small as you can.
At this point someone always asks: but don't we want progressive taxes? Shouldn't the rich pay a bigger share?
First, which kind of progressive do you mean? Because there are two, and almost nobody separates them.
Your marginal tax rate is what you pay on the next dollar you earn. Your effective tax rate is what you pay overall, as a share of everything you earn.
Most people assume you need progressive marginal rates, higher brackets for higher incomes, to get progressive effective rates. You don't.
Watch. Say there's a flat forty percent income tax. We're not proposing an income tax; it's just the simplest example. And every citizen gets a ten-thousand-dollar dividend.
Earn twelve thousand dollars. You pay four thousand eight hundred in tax, get ten thousand back, and take home seventeen thousand two hundred. Your effective tax rate is negative forty-three percent.
Earn fifty thousand: an effective rate of twenty percent. A hundred thousand: thirty percent. A million: thirty-nine percent.
One marginal rate. Effective rates that climb from deeply negative to nearly forty percent. About as progressive as most bracket systems, with no brackets at all.

And the marginal rate is the one that shapes incentives. It's what you weigh when you decide whether to take the extra shift, or whether to work for someone else at all, versus spending that time caring for your kids or an aging parent. Which brings us to the ugliest number in the welfare state.

Here's what that looks like in practice. PolicyEngine, which builds an open-source model of the American tax and benefit system, ran the numbers for a single parent in California with two kids, paying rent and childcare on a low wage. Double their pay. After lost benefits, lost tax credits and higher taxes, the family keeps only about a fifth of the extra. An effective marginal tax rate of nearly eighty percent.

In other words, a single parent near the poverty line can face a higher marginal tax rate than a billionaire. And at some incomes, losing a benefit all at once means earning more leaves you with less. That's the welfare cliff.

Remember the minimum wage fight? Under an eighty percent marginal rate, a worker keeps a fifth of every extra dollar. A fifteen-dollar minimum wage becomes a three-dollar one. People spend years fighting over the first number and never mention the second.
A flat dividend never shrinks when you earn more. No cliff. Every extra hour leaves you better off.
Which raises the obvious objection. Why should a millionaire get a ten-thousand-dollar check?

On net, they don't. You can't look at the check by itself. You have to look at the taxes that pay for it. Go back to our simple example, the forty percent flat income tax. The millionaire gets ten thousand dollars and pays four hundred thousand. Most of any tax goes to everything else government does, so count only the share that pays for the checks: everyone above roughly average income pays in more than they get back, and everyone below gets back more than they pay. Net, it's a transfer from richer to poorer. The millionaire's check is just bookkeeping.

And even if you decided the rich shouldn't get the check, how would you stop it? Pick an income cutoff, and everyone just above it falls off a cliff. Phase it out gradually instead, and you've built a higher marginal rate into the middle of the income ladder. Either way, you're back to means testing.
Max Ghenis of PolicyEngine has a phrase for this: means testing is a poor substitute for taxation. Phasing out a benefit as you earn more is a tax, aimed squarely at the poorest workers.
lines.say: Max Ghenniss of PolicyEngine has a phrase for this: means testing is a poor substitute for taxation. Phasing out a benefit as you earn more is a tax, aimed squarely at the poorest workers.

lines.text: If the goal is for the rich to pay more, use the tax itself. Raise the rate. Go from forty percent to fifty, and the millionaire pays a hundred thousand dollars more. That's ten times what taking away their check would recover. Seen this way, the check is really just a flat tax credit that's refundable: below a certain income, it pays you instead of charging you.

And remember, that income tax was only an example. In a system built on pollution and land taxes, the rich still pay more, because they consume more. Nearly everything they buy, from steak to golf to a second home, uses land and causes pollution somewhere along the way, and the prices they pay carry those costs.

Which exposes a confusion at the heart of most talk about wealth taxes. Wealth lumps together two different things. A mansion, a yacht, a private jet: that's consumption. Factories, farms, grocery stores: that's capital, making things for everyone else. Capital is the goose that lays the golden eggs. Someone rich on paper who lives modestly isn't consuming much at all, and when they cash out and spend, they pay. If progressive taxes are meant to narrow the gap in how people live, the target is consumption, not the goose.

And notice what the check doesn't need. No means test. No caseworkers verifying your income every few months. No paperwork, no penalty for a good month. Means testing is what creates the cliffs in the first place, and it takes a bureaucracy to run. The dividend replaces that patchwork. Stack it on top of the old phase-outs, and you'd keep the cliffs.

And the old worry that handouts make people lazy? The Congressional Budget Office reviewed the research in twenty twelve. By its central estimates, people respond roughly five times more strongly to how much of the next dollar they get to keep than to simply having more money. So what kills the incentive to work is the high marginal rate built into means testing, far more than the cash itself.
Graduated brackets have a quieter problem. They punish uneven income. Take a simple system: ten percent on your first fifty thousand dollars, thirty percent on anything above that.

Earn fifty thousand this year and fifty thousand next year, and you pay ten thousand dollars in total. Earn a hundred thousand this year and nothing next year, the same money, and you pay twenty thousand. Twice the tax for the same two years of income.

Who earns like that? Freelancers. Farmers. Construction workers. Artists. Anyone who works double shifts one year and cares for a newborn the next. The bracket system charges them extra for the timing of their paychecks, which has nothing to do with how rich they are.
A flat rate with a dividend doesn't care. Earn it all in one year or spread it across two, and over the two years you pay exactly the same.

By the way, if you still object to rich people getting a check, then you should object far more to every price cap and every "don't you dare raise prices." Hold Amazon's prices down, and every millionaire ordering online gets the discount too, with no tax on the other side clawing it back. Same objection. Much worse offender.
lines.say: [dryly] By the way, if you still object to rich people getting a check, then you should object far more to every price cap and every "don't you dare raise prices." Hold Amazon's prices down, and every millionaire ordering online gets the discount too, with no tax on the other side clawing it back. Same objection. Much worse offender.

lines.text: Rent control is worse still. In San Francisco, your discount depends on how long you've lived in your apartment and how much rents have risen since, with no check on what you earn. A tenant with a six-figure income who moved in a decade ago can pay a fraction of market rent, while a struggling family that just arrived pays full price.

Milton Friedman, not exactly a socialist, proposed something close to this dividend in nineteen sixty-two. He called it a negative income tax: a payment that shrinks as you earn more. Set the rate it shrinks at equal to the flat tax rate, and it's mathematically the same as a dividend plus a flat tax. Make it shrink much faster than that, and you've rebuilt the cliff.
So, back to New York.
If the city wants delivery workers to have more money, it can give them money. Out in the open, where voters can see the price, paid for by taxes that don't block useful trades.
Instead it hides the bill inside every online order in the city. And when the bill arrives, the mayor calls it greed.
That's the socialist toolkit in one move. Good intentions, delivered by gift card, paid for by a tax nobody can see, and blamed on someone else.

So here's our challenge, to anyone who defends rent control because people deserve a home. Fine. Let's take that as given: that's the values question. Now the engineering question. Why would you rather pin them to one apartment than give them the money to choose their own?
Pick any amount of redistribution you like. Zero, a little, a lot. Whatever it is, cash delivers it cheaper, and the people you meant to help end up with more.
So what do you call this? That's harder than it sounds.

Neoliberalism has been thrown around as an insult for so long that it barely means anything. Market socialism sounds close, but it still has socialism in the name, and it means something else entirely: worker-owned firms competing in markets. The clearest name might be the one from that Niskanen paper. The free-market welfare state.

And that naming problem is the whole problem in miniature. Without a word for sharing the pie without shrinking it, people assume there are only two teams: the one that wants to help people, and the one that wants markets to work. Most voters never hear the third option named, let alone explained.
Caring about the poor is the easy part. Doing the math is harder.
lines.say: [measured] Caring about the poor is the easy part. Doing the math is harder.

lines.text: Whatever you think people deserve, give it to them in cash.
